**My thinking:**

I've been farming this land in Quzhou for over 40 years. My father farmed it the same way. Around here, there's really only one system that makes sense — winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same fields. That's what everyone in the county does, and for good reason. Both crops have guaranteed buyers, the county cooperative helps with seeds and fertilizers, and I know exactly how to grow them. I'm not going to gamble on vegetables or cotton at my age — too much labor, too much price risk, and my knees can't handle that kind of bending work anymore.

I have 8 mu of flat land. I'll plant all of it in wheat this October and then flip it to maize in June after harvest. Same fields, back to back.

For wheat, I'll buy improved seed from the township seed station — probably Jimai 22 or Kenong 199, whatever they have. I won't bother with the premium hybrid wheat; it costs too much and the yield difference on my land isn't worth it. I'll apply compound fertilizer at planting and urea at the jointing stage. In this county we always irrigate before winter dormancy, then at jointing, then at heading — three times minimum. If it stays dry in April I'll add a fourth. I'll spray herbicide in November and hit the aphids and rust in April or May.

For maize, I'll direct-seed into the wheat stubble right after harvest — no plowing, just rotary seeding. Hybrid seed, Zhengdan 958 probably, from the same cooperative. Summer rains help so I only need one irrigation, maybe two in a bad year. I'll top-dress with urea at the 6-leaf stage and again at tasseling. One pesticide pass for corn borer or leaf blight if I see it.
